Permutation importance of a prediction function

Source: R/xpl.R
xpimp.Rd

How much worse a risk tool predicts when one of its inputs is made useless: the column is shuffled across the rows, which keeps its distribution but breaks its link with the outcome and with the other columns, and the loss of the predictions against y is measured again (Breiman 2001; Fisher, Rudin and Dominici 2019, who call the ratio the model reliance). Each column is shuffled nrep times and the mean and the standard deviation of the increases are reported.

Usage

xpimp(
  x,
  f,
  y,
  nrep = 10,
  loss = c("se", "ae"),
  ratio = FALSE,
  seed = 1,
  lctl = list()
)

# S3 method for class 'xpimp'
print(x, ...)

Arguments

x

The rows at which to predict: a numeric matrix, its column names those f sees, no missing values.

f

The prediction function: a function of a numeric matrix returning one finite number per row, or the names of learners of suplrn() ("glm", "lasso", "ridge", "enet", "forest").

y

The outcome at the rows of x: one finite number per row.

nrep

The shuffles of each column: one whole number from 1.

loss

"se", the squared error (the Brier score for a 0/1 outcome), or "ae", the absolute error.

ratio

FALSE for the increase of the loss, the loss after shuffling less the loss before; TRUE for their ratio.

seed

The seed of the shuffles: one number, at least 0.

lctl

The settings of the learners named in f: a list named by arguments of suplrn() (fam, nfold, fold, disc, alpha, nlam, nfin, ntree, mtry, seed); empty for a function.

...

Not used by print().

Value

An object of class xpimp, a list: imp, a data frame with one row per column of x (term, imp the mean increase or ratio, sd its standard deviation over the shuffles); base, the loss before shuffling; rep, the increase or ratio of every shuffle (one row per column, one column per shuffle); perm, the shuffles (an array of nrow(x) rows, nrep columns and one slice per column of x: perm[i, r, j] is the row whose value of column j row i takes in shuffle r); loss and ratio.

Details

f is the prediction function: an R function that takes a numeric matrix with the columns of x and returns one prediction per row, or the names of learners of the package, fitted to x and y by suplrn() with the settings in lctl (one learner is that learner, as rfor() or least squares; several are their stack). The function is called once, on the rows of x followed by every shuffled copy, so a learner is fitted once. With learners the loss is measured on the rows they were fitted to; for the loss on new rows, give f as a function and x and y as the new rows.

The shuffles are drawn in the compiled core from seed, the same on every platform; perm returns them, so that every value can be checked.

References

Breiman, L. (2001). Random forests. Machine Learning, 45(1), 5-32. doi:10.1023/A:1010933404324

Fisher, A., Rudin, C. and Dominici, F. (2019). All models are wrong, but many are useful: learning a variable's importance by studying an entire class of prediction models simultaneously. Journal of Machine Learning Research, 20(177), 1-81.

See also

xppdp(), xpale(), xpcp() and xpshap() for the shape of an input's effect; fair() and calaud() for the audit of a risk tool's scores.

Examples

set.seed(1)
x <- cbind(prior = rpois(200, 2), age = runif(200, 18, 60),
           noise = rnorm(200))
y <- 0.3 * x[, "prior"] - 0.02 * x[, "age"] + rnorm(200, sd = 0.5)
f <- function(m) 0.3 * m[, "prior"] - 0.02 * m[, "age"]
xpimp(x, f, y, nrep = 5)
#> xpimp: permutation importance, 5 shuffles per column; loss se (increase), 0.2852 before shuffling
#>   term       imp         sd
#>  prior 0.3260732 0.02932846
#>    age 0.1047989 0.01306672
#>  noise 0.0000000 0.00000000
xpimp(x, "glm", y, nrep = 5, lctl = list(nfold = 2))
#> xpimp: permutation importance, 5 shuffles per column; loss se (increase), 0.284 before shuffling
#>   term          imp          sd
#>  prior 3.469121e-01 0.031564597
#>    age 1.071655e-01 0.013107077
#>  noise 6.448013e-06 0.000732987
